zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Review reference: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, National Institute for Japanese Language and Linguistics (NINJAL), Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510; CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The supplied lexical index was consulted as a secondary aid; the transcription and English review notes are scan-based reviewer work, not a reproduction of that dataset.

lines.note: The first noru completes the example begun on the preceding page; the gloss is to ride. Vmauo noru specifies riding a horse, and its Portuguese explanation continues through the printed An- at the right edge.
The horse-riding explanation finishes here. Funeni noru introduces boarding a vessel; Embar- is the visible physical-line division of the following Portuguese verb, not a complete word.

This completes embarcarſe and introduces riding in a palanquin or carriage. The scan's damaged or abbreviated-looking curum. is retained rather than silently supplying the expected final a of kuruma; the period-like trace is visible, but the underlying last letter is not secure.

The preceding example is translated as travelling in a palanquin or carriage. Coxi is a Japanese vehicle name embedded in the Portuguese gloss here, unlike its occurrence in the Japanese example above.
A separate nori/noru entry concerns a sword becoming bent rather than mounting a vehicle. The Japanese example makes the sword the subject; En- begins entortarſe on the next line.
This completes the gloss that the sword becomes bent. Catana is retained as the printed Japanese loan or term inside the Portuguese sentence, not converted to a modern spelling.

runs.text: Noriagari, u, atta. i, Cazauyeni noru.

lines.note: Noriagari is explained by taking the windward position; Cazauyeni noru is the Japanese paraphrase. The following Portuguese explanation begins with Eſ-, completed as eſtar below.

runs.text: tar no nauio da parte donde vem o vento ſe he

lines.note: The gloss locates the person on the side of a ship from which the wind comes. The conditional phrase at the end carries into the next line, so this is not a separate definition.

The nautical explanation ends with sailing on a bowline or placing oneself to windward. The printed abalrauento is retained, including its letter order and lack of an intervening space, rather than modernized to a barlavento.

runs.text: O embarcarſe de diuerſas partes, ou

lines.note: Noriai describes travelling together in a vessel, with people coming from different places. The Portuguese alternative introduced by ou is completed on the next physical line.
This supplies the other half of the gloss: various people embark together. The printed double-s form in peßoas is retained; this short continuation does not begin a new entry.
The headword is a shared passenger vessel, noriai no fune. The scan clearly has fune, correcting the draft's fone; the Portuguese description explains who boards it on the next line.
The vessel carries people from different places. This completes the preceding noun phrase and confirms that fune denotes a boat rather than an unrelated Japanese word.

The scan reads Noriaino fito, correcting the draft's missing n in Noriaio. The Japanese paraphrase denotes people who have come aboard together; the caron in Noriyǒta and the division Paßa- are retained.
This completes Paßageiros: passengers from different places. It is the Portuguese explanation of the people in the preceding headword, not another vessel entry.
Noricacari/norikakaru means to put or throw oneself onto something. The object of the Portuguese preposition ſobre continues on the next line, before two concrete examples.
The general object is some thing. The Japanese example begins with being on top of a person's chest; the printed vyeni is retained rather than normalized to modern ue ni.
Nori cacaru completes that example, translated as straddling or placing oneself upon the chest. The printed space within the Japanese compound is retained; the Portuguese object continues below.
The first example ends with a man's chest. A second example concerns climbing onto or into a castle; Xironinori is printed together and ca- is genuinely divided at the line end.
Caru completes the Japanese verb begun above. The Portuguese gives climbing and leaping inside a fortress, which establishes xiro as the castle term in the example.

This noun describes a riding animal fitted with side loads on both sides. Coſtais belongs to the Portuguese explanation; the next line completes dambas as partes before giving the Japanese construction.
The gloss completes both sides and then gives preparing a horse in this noricaqe arrangement. The visible A- starts Amanhar on the next line; it is not a detached initial or new entry.

runs.text: manhar o caualo deſta maneira que leue dam-

lines.note: The horse is prepared so that it carries the load in the arrangement just described. The right-edge dam- is retained as the beginning of dambas across the line break.

runs.text: bas as partes fato pera caualgar alguem no meo.

lines.note: The explanation specifies baggage on both sides, leaving the middle for a rider. Fato here is baggage or belongings in the source explanation, not the modern abstract sense of fact.
This is the verbal entry noricaqe/noricaquru, distinct from the preceding load arrangement. The Portuguese begins with driving or launching the horse onward; the object follows on the next line.

runs.text: o caualo por cima dalguem, ou apos alguem.

lines.note: The horse is urged over someone or after someone. The two alternatives explain the direction of the action rather than two unrelated meanings of the headword.
The boat example extends the same verb to bringing a vessel against another or ramming. Funeuo noricaquru is a standalone Japanese example; the Portuguese preposition com takes its object below.
This supplies the vessel in the preceding gloss, completing abalroar com nauio. Although very short, the row is genuine text and remains a separate indented physical line.
Noricaſanari describes many people getting onto something or crowding together. The printed long s in the headword is retained; the object of ſobre continues below.

runs.text: algũa couſa, ou estarem muitos juntos, &c.

lines.note: This finishes the general explanation, adding the sense of many people gathered together. The draft's estarem is retained for the close italic st forms rather than imposing a new allograph globally.
The example describes people insisting on going first despite the danger of a bridge. The negative phrase is divided iua / zu without a printed terminal hyphen; no hyphen is supplied.

This finishes the crowded-bridge example and cites Taif., followed by the Portuguese book abbreviation. The citation label is treated as a whole Roman term rather than splitting its terminal punctuation into the following italic span.

runs.text: 6. Cada hum aquem primeiro auia de paßar

lines.note: The citation specifies book 6. The translation begins with each person trying to be first to cross; the printed aquem and historical auia are retained without editorial modernization.

runs.text: ſem ter deuer com o perigo da ponte, ſubirão hũs

lines.note: The people disregard the bridge's danger and climb one upon another. Deuer is preserved as printed in this older expression, and the plural hũs continues syntactically into the next row.

runs.text: ſobre outros, ou muito juntos, & apinhoados.

lines.note: The explanation ends with people on top of each other, close together and crowded. The scan reads juntos, not the draft's funtos; the descender and the sense both support the correction.
Noricauari means transferring oneself to another conveyance. The visible embar- starts the vessel term, followed on the next line by a riding animal as another possible conveyance.
This completes embarcação and gives changing to another mount as an alternative. The line belongs to the preceding transfer verb, not to the closely related headword below.
Noricaye/norikayuru concerns changing the horse or vessel. The Portuguese object beginning a continues into embarcação below; the headword's y and full inflectional notation are retained.

runs.text: embarcação paßandoſe de hũa a outra.

lines.note: The gloss explains transferring from one vessel to another. The scan has continuous embarcação, correcting the draft's internal space in embar cação; hũa retains the printed nasal mark.
Norichigaye describes passing each other or missing one another while travelling. The source divides em / barcação without a terminal hyphen after em, and that absence is preserved.

runs.text: barcação paßando hũa polla outra, ou a caua-

lines.note: The vessels pass one another; travelling on horseback is then added as an alternative. The right-edge word is caua-, correcting the draft's eaua-, and its visible hyphen remains.
This finishes caualo and the definition of passing one another in transit. It is a short continuation, with neither an omitted headword nor an extra paragraph boundary.
Noricoroxi means killing a horse by riding it too hard. The explanation begins running the horse, with the printed nasal abbreviation and terminal hyphen retained in corrẽ-.
This completes corrẽdoo and adds exhausting the horse excessively. The doubled o in the attached-object forms is the source's spelling, not a duplication introduced by transcription.
Noricoxi means passing over or across something on horseback. The following example is continued at the top of column 2; this headword is not the fatal over-riding verb above.

The Japanese example begins with these men and even a slight wound. Vſude corresponds to the minor injury mentioned in the Portuguese translation across the column break, supporting the printed long-s reading.

The sentence continues that they crossed the river very quietly without receiving even that injury. Separate second-pass enlargement shows an open c without a descender in vcuaide, restoring the supplied spelling rather than the first-pass q interpretation. The older form is not regularized; nori- continues as coxi in column 2.
Coxi completes nori- from the foot of column 1. Tac. is the source citation, and the Portuguese translation begins with these men receiving no injury; the column break does not create a fresh entry.

runs.text: nem hũa pequena ferida paßarão a ribeira muito

lines.note: The men crossed the river without even a small wound. The source uses the historical past-tense spelling paßarão; the nasal marks in hũa and the original physical division are retained.

runs.text: deuagar. ¶ Item, Paßar por cima de cor-

lines.note: The crossing was very slow or deliberate. A further sense follows: going over bodies or other objects, with the printed cor- continued as corpos below.

runs.text: pos mortos, ou outras couſas ainda que ſeja a pè.

lines.note: This completes the extension to passing over dead bodies or other things, even on foot. It broadens the preceding horse-riding sense rather than changing the headword or beginning another entry.
Noricoye/norikoyuru means going over something. The damaged but recoverable Portuguese word is cima, correcting cita; the object and the specification that this is on foot continue below.
The gloss is completed as passing over some thing on foot. The printed accent in pè is retained rather than converted to the modern acute-accent spelling.
Noricuchi is illustrated by the good or bad responsiveness of a horse to the bridle. Yoi and varui are alternatives within the Japanese example, and vma is carried onto the following row.

runs.text: Caualo bom, ou mao do freo.

lines.note: Vma completes the example: a horse good or bad under the bit. The final B. is an upright usage label in the scan, so it is separated from the italic Portuguese explanation; the subsequent Meliùs introduces a preferred expression.

The dictionary recommends Cuchino yoi or varui vma as the better expression for a horse's response to the bit. The Japanese wording is a standalone alternative example, not an embedded Portuguese term for typeface marking.
This verb is exemplified by storming and breaking down a castle. The scan reads Xirouo, correcting Xurouo; the following no- begins the example's verb across the physical line boundary.
Ricuzzuſu completes the Japanese verb. The explanation begins with forcibly climbing or entering the fortress; the destructive result appears in the next short continuation.
The result is destroying the fortress. The printed attached-object spelling destruila is retained, including the draft's st representation for the close italic ligature.
Norifanachi concerns dismounting and letting the horse go. The inflection tçu and the visible bo- at the right edge are retained; botar is completed on the next row.
This completes botar and adds leaving the horse behind. It explains the releasing component of the preceding Japanese compound after dismounting.
Norifanaxi is given the same meaning as Norifanachi immediately above. The different headword ending and inflectional series remain distinct; Idem does not justify merging the entries.
Norifazzuxi means failing in the intended boarding or mounting. The dictionary prints the past form zzuita, which is retained; embarca- is a real right-edge word division.

runs.text: ção em que hum ſe auia de embarcar, ou deixar

lines.note: One possibility is missing the vessel one was supposed to board. The alternative introduced by ou deixar continues into failing to mount the intended horse on the next line.

runs.text: de caualgar no caualo em que auia de caualgar,

lines.note: This gives the parallel failure to ride the horse one intended to ride. The repeated caualgar is part of the explanation and is not an OCR duplication.

runs.text: ou cair no mar, &c. indo pera ſe embarcar.

lines.note: A further example is falling into the sea while attempting to board. This remains within the same mishap or failure-to-board entry; pera and the printed punctuation are preserved.

Norigaye denotes a horse led alongside or kept as a spare mount. The gloss adestra is retained as printed together; the Japanese example repeats the headword with a visible hyphen before its object marker on the next line.
The example means having spare horses led along. This line prints a deſtra with a space, unlike adestra above; that local spacing difference is preserved rather than harmonized.
Norigocoro concerns how a horse feels or handles when ridden. The example contrasts good and bad, with its final noun vma supplied on the next physical line.

runs.text: Caualo bom, ou mao pera caualgar, &

lines.note: The horse is good or bad to ride. The final ampersand introduces the additional consideration of directing it, completed in the following Portuguese continuation.
The gloss ends with manoeuvring the horse in any direction. This specifies handling under the rider, distinguishing the entry from the earlier narrower description of response to the bit.
Noridaxi begins with taking a vessel out after boarding it. The Portuguese reads Embarcandoſe, correcting the draft's Einbarcandoſe; the apparent in was the divided strokes of m.

runs.text: embarcação, ou faze la ſair. Vt,

lines.note: The vessel is put out or made to depart. The printed faze la is retained without adding a modern clitic hyphen, and Funeuo begins the Japanese example completed below.
The boat example finishes, followed by setting out on a horse. The damaged Ca- at the right edge remains readable with the following ualgando; no word has been clipped from the crop.
The gloss completes caualgando and explains riding out with the horse. It supplies the equestrian parallel to launching or taking out the boat above.

The headword is Noriire, with both i letters visible, correcting Norire. The rider directs the horse into some place; the inflectional form uru confirms that this is the entering compound rather than a separate nori noun.

runs.text: lo por algũa parte, a embarcação, &c.

lines.note: This completes caualo and extends the entry to directing a vessel into a place. The source's compressed coordination is preserved rather than rewriting the Portuguese to make the ellipsis explicit.
Norimauaxi means making a mount or vehicle go around. The horse example starts here and continues through the visible caua- / lo division.

runs.text: lo, ou embarcado fazer rodear a Fune.

lines.note: The alternative is making a boat turn while aboard it. Fune is a Japanese vessel term embedded within Portuguese here and is retained with its printed capital F and italic treatment.
Norimodoxi means making the conveyance return. The right-edge em- begins embarcação below; it is a different physical division from the unhyphenated em on column 1 line 40.

runs.text: barcação, ou o caualo, ẽbarcado, ou caualgado.

lines.note: The return may be by vessel or horse, while aboard or mounted. The source abbreviates the nasal in ẽbarcado here, unlike the fully spelled embarcação at the beginning of the same sentence.
Norimono is defined specifically as a litter or palanquin in this entry. The definition should not be expanded to every modern sense of vehicle, even though related headwords cover boats and horses.
Norimucai means going out to meet someone by boat or on horseback. Both inflectional carons are visibly downward-pointing and are retained, as is the division ca- before ualgando.
This completes the horseback alternative and the action of going to meet someone. It belongs to the preceding encounter verb, not to the adjustment-of-position entry that follows.

The damaged headword is read as Norinauori, correcting Nuxinauori: the surviving letters and the following explanation support adjusting one's position to right the vessel. The initial ori portion is rubbed, so this incorporated reading remains a nonblocking caveat.

runs.text: uio com mudar o lugar na embarcação, ou con-

lines.note: The boat is righted by changing one's place aboard. A parallel adjustment on horseback begins with con-, continued as concertarſe on the next line.

runs.text: certarſe milhor na caualgadura que vão os coſtais

lines.note: The rider adjusts position on the mount so that the side loads sit properly. The older comparative spelling milhor and the nasal in vão are retained as printed.
This completes the statement that the side loads should be straight or balanced. It is the end of the rider-position entry and must not be attached to the next headword's training sense.

Norinauoxi concerns training or correcting a horse by riding it. The scan does not support the draft's caron in Norinauǒxi; the unaccented o agrees with the visible example below, and the spurious accent is removed.

runs.text: tirar lhe algũas manhas com o caualgar. Vt,

lines.note: The explanation adds removing some of the horse's bad habits through riding. The printed separated clitic tirar lhe is retained; Vt introduces the Japanese example on the next row.

This Japanese example means correcting or retraining the horse through riding. Its norinauoſu spelling supplies a clear local comparison for the damaged headword above, without adding any kana to canonical text.
Noriſoconai means doing the riding or navigating badly. The carons in its inflection are visible and retained; the Portuguese errando introduces the nature of the mistake below.

runs.text: no modo, & ordem de caualgar, ou nauegar

lines.note: The mistake may concern the manner or order of riding, or navigation. The sentence continues to the last body row; there is no extra headword at the page foot.

The final alternative is navigating badly and going wrong on the journey. The compact malerrando is retained from the aligned draft because the source's narrow spacing does not firmly establish a separate word break; the catchword below is separate furniture.
